title: X Files creator Chris Carter on Mulder-Scully reunion rumours, a Millennium reboot — and his new movie
summary: Chris Carter spoke to CBC News about the future, and the past, of The X Files and his new, self-financed feature film.

image.caption: TV producer and director Chris Carter is seen at the ACE Eddie Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Jan. 29, 2016. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Chris Carter has a complicated relationship with nostalgia.

Not that looking back has been a bad strategy for the American director, who is currently shopping around a new film, Queens for a Day. Given that he's the creator and showrunner of the incredibly successful and now resurgent sci-fi series The X Files, people’s tendency to look back has mostly worked out for him. Even if it keeps him coming back to something he finished nearly 30 years ago.

"It's funny, I'm a nostalgic person by nature. I look back at time past and while I can't avoid recognizing the bad things, the good things are always what stand out," said Carter, who shared that he's actually considering making a documentary about nostalgia, rooted in his up-and-down life and experiences.
"Really, if I were to visit the places that were formative for me and meant something to me, I'm gonna have to acknowledge the good with the bad."

Lately, it seems mostly good. There’s the upcoming Ryan Coogler reboot of The X Files with two new stars, which Disney subsidiary Hulu picked up for a series order in October. For an added boost of nostalgia, Coogler credited Carter as executive producer — despite the fact he's not creatively involved.

From left, actor Gillian Anderson, director Chris Carter, producer Frank Spotnitz and actor David Duchovny attend the world premiere of The X Files: I Want To Believe in Hollywood on July 23, 2008. (Stephen Shugerman/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, the Sinners director went to the wistful lengths of filming the show's pilot in dreary, moody Vancouver, returning the series to the place where Carter created it.

But according to Hans Dayal, production manager caucus representative for the Directors Guild of Canada's BC branch, the rest of the series will be filmed in Chicago in the spring. Star Himesh Patel said Coogler was still writing the show as of mid-November, while representatives for Disney did not respond to a query by CBC.

"I don't know about that decision," Carter said about the reboot's potential move away from Vancouver, before revealing he hasn't so much as read the scripts. "I decided not to read it, because I didn't want to have the experience spoiled: of sitting down with ... a bowl of popcorn and watching it like everyone else."

What's behind the sustained popularity of the original show? Carter doesn't deny that younger audiences' appetite could be fuelled by X Files' themes around questioning authority — and, more literally, the government.

Looking back at the original production, he describes himself as "a child of Watergate." He believed, and believes, there were conspiracies born of it. And from that belief, he says, grew everything from The X Files to Queens for a Day, which he calls a "fist in the air in protest for what's going on in the U.S. right now."

items: The X-Files began filming in Vancouver 30 years ago. It became a cultural touchstone and local point of pride

blocks.text: He says the refocused attention on The X Files stems from other factors, too. There is the obvious appeal of David Duchovny's Mulder and Gillian Anderson's Scully, Carter's "ideal of a man-woman relationship" based in platonic love but without fear of disagreeing with or doubting one another.
"It was an ideal that I chose to write about and has lasted through the decades now," he said. "If it weren't for that relationship, we could really be just another sci-fi show."
Dealing with fan yearning

Fans can't seem to shed their nostalgia for that pair, either. After months of speculation, Anderson suggested she had read Coogler's pilot script before it was shot and Duchovny revealed he had spoken to Coogler about the possibility of appearing in it.

Carter has also felt the fan yearning. Earlier this month, he said in an interview that his own 2016 X Files revival set up the potential for a show or movie bringing Mulder and Scully back together. And when he made a passing comment that he would like to make something like that one day, a raft of headlines followed, hinting it might happen.

He throws cold water on the seriousness with which some have taken the remark. Duchovny and Anderson have gone off to other things and there’s no current studio involvement. And the Coogler reboot has already headed into production.

"I don't want to compete with it. I don't want to overshadow it in any way," Carter said. "Even the fact that I'm talking to you about it now is a little troubling to me, because I want that show to come out and shine."
Duchovny, left, and Anderson appear as Mulder and Scully in an image from the original X Files series. (Fox/Getty Images)
The project he's more invested in revisiting is Millennium, his dark crime-horror series, which was filmed on the same Vancouver soundstages as The X Files, and ran from 1996 to 1999.
"It ended too soon. I actually chose to pull the plug too soon on the show. The show had lots more life in it," he said.

Carter says it was his ill-advised focus on launching the one-and-done series Harsh Realm that convinced the network, Fox, to cancel Millennium. And now, like everyone else, he's banking on the past for his future — working on a reboot pilot that he would also aim to shoot in Vancouver.
New film
And then there's Queens for a Day, which will show at the Whistler Film Festival in December and is currently hitting a smattering of individual theatres elsewhere.

It's a serious departure for the longtime studio-based TV producer. First, he made the entirely self-financed film from an unproduced 30-year-old script written by his wife, author and screenwriter Dori Carter, loosely based on her relationship with her mother.

Second is the genre. He describes it as a politically charged, nightmare reinterpretation of Dickens's A Christmas Carol. A right-wing newscaster who's forced to live through her mother's youth — including giving birth to herself — quickly realizes that her rose-coloured view of America's past doesn't necessarily square with reality.
A still from Chris Carter's new film, Queens for a Day. (Chris Carter)
On paper, the personal touches are still there, such as the dark hints at the supernatural. Carter insists on calling the film a "comedy nightmare" or "horror fable" rather than true horror.
"Horror scares people; there are people who won't go to see a horror movie."
There was also a return to the same Vancouver sound stages for filming.
"I brought this to Canada without hesitation," he said, pointing to Alberta director of photography Craig Wrobleski as the only crew member not from B.C.

blocks.text: But there is also change. There is the comedy at the heart of Queens for a Day. There is the unabashed political celebration, as Carter describes it, which is serendipitously in line with the recent "blue wave" in the U.S. midterms. So in line, and in protest of the recent political climate, that he says it would have been impossible for an American studio to make the film.

It's all a mix of forward and backward in his description. Forward in how he views nostalgia, a "glossy look at the past" that is "always dangerous." It makes him want to try new things like Queens for a Day. After finishing The X Files, genre television or movies were the last things he wanted to do.
But there are more mundane realities, too. Such as being constantly asked about a show he created nearly 40 years ago, while promoting his new film.
Surprisingly, it has never bothered him.

"I'm not hindered by it. [The X Files] certainly provides a knock, and an opening, and a door and a greeting. But that's about all it is for," he said. "It's part of my portfolio, if you will. I still have to produce the goods."
